newsitem.title: UK: N. Irish Catholics await Major on IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: N. Irish Catholics await Major on IRA ceasefire.

text.p: Irish nationalists said on Monday they were waiting for a response from British Prime Minister John Major to the terms for a possible new IRA guerrilla ceasefire.

Each claimed that the other had to make the first move to help bring about a new halt to attacks proposed by John Hume, a moderate Northern Ireland nationalist, and the Irish Republican Army's political arm Sinn Fein.
"The ball is very firmly in the court of the British government. We are awaiting the response of John Major ... there is nothing more we can do," said Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin.
A spokeswoman for Major said the prime minister's position remained as on Sunday when Northern Ireland minister Michael Ancram insisted that "the ball is firmly in the IRA's court".
She played down media reports that Major would issue a response this week. The IRA has fought a bomb-and bullet campaign for decades to end British rule of Northern Ireland.

Hume is believed to be suggesting that Sinn Fein be allowed into flagging peace talks debating the future of Northern Ireland if the IRA renews its ceasefire and Britain drops demands that the guerrillas disarm immediately.
Standing on the sidelines, leaders of the pro-British Protestant "Loyalists" threatened to walk out of the talks if their Republican rivals were allowed in on the basis of a "wonky" IRA ceasefire.
"If Sinn Fein comes to the table on their own terms then the Democratic Unionists (DUP) will not be at the table -- full stop," said DUP leader Ian Paisley.
Sinn Fein has been barred from joining the talks because of the IRA's refusal to renew a 17-month ceasefire it abandoned in February by setting off bombs in Britain.
The Loyalist politicians are involved in the negotiations because their guerrilla wings are still honouring a two-year truce, originally called to match the IRA's.
The Loyalists, fighting to keep Northern Ireland under British rule, have accused Major of doing secret deals with the IRA to get a new truce. Both Britain and Sinn Fein deny this.
Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist SDLP, and Sinn Fein also want "goodwill gestures" from Britain such as the release of Republican prisoners from British jails.
Ancram indicated over the weekend that if the IRA resumed a "credible and dependable" ceasefire, Sinn Fein would be allowed to take part in the talks.
The IRA abandoned its ceasefire, accusing the British government of intransigence in its demands that the guerrillas disarm in advance of the talks.

George Mitchell, the former U.S. senator who chairs the talks, had proposed that arms decommissioning be one of the issues the talks addressed, but Major rejected this, insisting disarmament should come first.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Monday he believed there was growing support among Republicans for a new ceasefire.

"I believe there is a strong internal debate taking place in the Republican movement and the policy of violence is being re-assessed and there is a growing recognition violence is not a way of solving problems," he told the Irish parliament.
